To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
Fet-A, which impairs insulin signaling is secreted by the liver and adipose tissue.
FetA is a hepatokine that is secreted by adipose tissue and is increased in obesity.
fetuin-A is a novel hepatokine that is secreted in the liver, circulates in the blood and is deposited in the subcutaneous adipocyte.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification of the molecular pathways that regulate the expression of the adipokine fetuin-A in the adipose tissue.
understanding the mechanisms by which the liver and adipose tissue regulate glucose homeostasis.
the identification, characterization, and regulation of novel adipokines.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
Fet-A is a hepatokine, adipokine, and a cytokine.
Fet-A is an adipokine, hepatokine and a lipokine.
Fet-A is an adipokine and hepatokine and that it plays a major role in the development of metabolic syndrome.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
Fet-A is a hepatokine that acts on adipose tissue and that adipose tissue is also a source of Fet-A.
Fet-A is a hepatokine and adipokine and that it is involved in the pathophysiology of metabolic syndrome.
Fet-A is a novel adipokine and adipokine-like protein, that is increased in both circulating and adipose tissue in obesity and Metabolic Syndrome.
The main takeaway from our work is that
Fet-A is a marker of metabolic dysfunction in the absence of diabetes or cardiovascular disease.
Fet-A is an adipokine that is increased in metabolic syndrome.
Fet-A is a novel adipokine that is upregulated in the adipose tissue of patients with Metabolic syndrome.
